questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The workload is quite heavy, so think carefully when choosing your classes. I took both bachelor’s- and graduate-level courses (L3 and M1), and there is a significant difference in difficulty between the two. As a bachelor’s student, I probably wouldn’t recommend taking M1 courses, especially if you’re not very confident in your French. The lectures are very fast-paced and last two hours with no breaks. Same with the exercise classes.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The classes were definitely interesting, but their quality depended a lot on the professors, who could be more or less pleasant. There really wasn’t a system in place to support you if you fell behind or became overwhelmed—you had to work a lot and mostly on your own, unless you took the initiative to establish a study group.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The bachelor’s courses are quite similar in level to those in Copenhagen, except that you are expected to memorize everything. All exams are closed-book and include a large number of questions. There isn’t much time for reflection—when you see an exercise, you need to know almost immediately how to solve it.
The M1 courses are much more intense and difficult, so you should be genuinely interested in the subject if you decide to take them. Make sure you have the necessary prerequisites: even if the recommended courses have names similar to ones you have taken at UCPH, it is not guaranteed that the content will be the same. There is very little time to catch up, so you need to study consistently, as most courses include multiple tests throughout the semester.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It’s more intense. Lectures and exercise classes last two hours with no breaks. There isn’t much time to work on problems on your own, and the instructor goes through them quite quickly, so you really need to take time afterward to review them yourself. I didn’t have any assignments to hand in, but each class had two tests—a midterm and a final exam—so it gets quite intense. You have to stay on top of your classes at all times.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: L'art d'être spectateur. You get to go to the theater and see shows for free. It is also a good way to meet other students outside of your field or Erasmus.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Paris is a great city, filled with museums, clubs, and bars. There are also many excellent smaller concert venues.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Ask if they want to go to the library or study together. Most students are very academically focused, so socializing isn’t always easy—everyone is stressed.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: French bureaucracy.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The directness in communication.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: The educational system is quite different, so be prepared to work a lot, or be very mindful when choosing courses. Paris is a great city, so try to find a balance between academics and enjoying yourself. It’s easy to get caught up in the demands of classes, but make sure to take time to take advantage of everything else the city has to offer. It’s quite normal to feel overwhelmed.
